notes: \cpara{Introduces the parable from Carl Sagan's \textsc{The Demon-Haunted World}, chapter ``The Dragon in My Garage.'' The summary is fair: in Sagan the claimant, asked for proof, says ``I neglected to mention that she's an invisible dragon.''}

\cpara{Sagan does make this point. He imagines that ``things had gone otherwise'': footprints appear in the flour and the infrared detector ``reads off-scale,'' and then ``you must now acknowledge that there's something here.''}
\cpara{Retells the claimant's excuses for each test proposed: inaudible, does not breathe, permeable to flour.}

\cpara{The post's own contribution, and it goes beyond Sagan. Sagan draws from the excuses that ``something funny is going on inside my head,'' and asks ``what convinced me,'' but does not ask what the claimant expects. The post draws a sharper inference: to excuse the right tests in advance, the claimant must already expect them to come out empty.}

\cpara{The philosophers are not named, and the assumption the post gives them is not theirs. Their question is the ``static paradox'' of self-deception, which the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} states as ``How can a person simultaneously hold contradictory beliefs?'' It asks how contradictory beliefs can coexist, not whether the brain has room for more than one. Among the answers it lists from before 2007 are Robert Audi's (1982, 1988), that the self-deceived person sincerely avows what they do not believe, and Eric Funkhouser's (2005), which it summarizes as: ``they believe that they believe that p.'' These are close to the answer this post goes on to give.}

\cpara{Grants that the rule of ``Making Beliefs Pay Rent,'' posted the day before, does not reach this case: the dragon belief connects easily to what one would see in the garage. The problem is not that the belief floats.}

\cpara{Introduces Dennett's term with two examples: a child who doubts Santa Claus but thinks they are supposed to believe, and a contradictory statement, a sky both ``perfectly blue and perfectly green,'' which, the post says, is easier to think it good to believe than to believe. The post credits Dennett for the term. I could not check the paraphrase of Dennett against the book.}

\cpara{The post's addition to Dennett: a person who only believes in belief cannot admit it to themselves, because what is virtuous is to believe. The first sentence is hedged with ``I think''; the rest (``Nobody will admit'') is stated as fact about everyone, with no evidence.}

\cpara{An aside: mathematical logic distinguishes a proposition, a proof of it, and a proof that it is provable; the post lists the parallel distinctions among believing, wanting and believing that you believe.}
\cpara{Lists kinds of belief in belief: an explicit sentence recited to oneself, fear of public ridicule, and a flinch that protects a self-image as ``the glorious discoverer of the dragon.''}
\cpara{Claims that wordless images, flinches and unacknowledged desires ``account for as much of ourselves as words.'' It is offered as a general truth, without support.}

\cpara{Sets the post's wider concept of belief against Dennett (``While I disagree with Dennett \ldots\ But we need a wider concept of belief''). Dennett had drawn a similar line himself. In \textsc{Brainstorms} (1978) he separated beliefs, dispositions to act that animals also have, from ``opinions,'' commitments to sentences, and suggested that self-deception arises when the two diverge. I have this from Keith Frankish's account (\textsc{Philosophical Psychology}, 1998); I could not read Dennett's chapter, or check whether \textsc{Breaking the Spell} uses the distinction.}
\cpara{Illustrates wordless belief: you expect no dragon when you open a door without ever thinking the sentence ``There is no dragon in my garage.''}
\cpara{Illustrates wordless belief in belief: to protect the belief one need only flinch from admitting it is gone, not think a sentence about wanting it.}
\cpara{Ends with the post's practical sign, hedged with ``it would seem'': excuses made in advance show that belief and belief in belief have come apart. It is the one observable test in the post.}
\cpara{Cites Dennett's book on religion, the source of the term.}
\cpara{Says, as fact and without support, that a rationalist would congratulate the claimant for admitting the mistake, and that ridicule is likelier for going on.}
\cpara{Adds that belief in belief can still interfere when the belief itself is not fully confident.}
